breakfast.name: Musakhan (Sumac Chicken on Bread)
instructions: Caramelize onions with sumac in olive oil
Brown chicken
Place bread on platter, top with onions
Lay chicken on top
Garnish with toasted pine nuts
breakfast.description: Palestine's national dish — sumac-onion chicken on taboon bread.

breakfast.name: Hummus bil Lahm
instructions: Make hummus, spread on plate
Brown lamb with spices
Spoon lamb over hummus
Top with pine nuts and olive oil
breakfast.description: Smooth hummus topped with spiced lamb and pine nuts.

breakfast.name: Foul Mudammas (Fava Bean Stew)
ingredients: Dried fava beans (soaked overnight, cooked until soft)
instructions: Foul mudammas is Palestine's everyday breakfast — fava beans mashed with lemon and olive oil
The fava beans are soaked overnight and simmered until soft — then partially mashed
The olive oil is essential — Palestine's olive oil is among the world's finest
Crush garlic into the beans, add lemon juice, cumin, generous olive oil
Top with chopped tomato, onion, and parsley — the freshness cuts the earthiness
Scoop with pita bread — the bread is the utensil
Foul is the common people's breakfast — affordable, protein-rich, sustaining
Palestinian olive oil from the West Bank (Nablus, Jenin) is prized — ancient groves still producing
breakfast.description: Palestine's everyday morning stew — fava beans simmered soft, partially mashed with lemon juice, crushed garlic, cumin, and generous Palestinian olive oil (from ancient West Bank groves — among the world's finest). Topped with chopped tomato, onion, and parsley. Scooped with pita. Affordable, protein-rich, sustaining — the common people's breakfast.

breakfast.name: Labneh with Za'atar and Olive Oil
instructions: Labneh with za'atar is the Palestinian breakfast that captures the entire cuisine in one bite
Labneh: yoghurt strained until thick and creamy — spread on a plate
Drizzle olive oil generously — make a well in the labneh and pool the oil
Sprinkle za'atar — the blend of dried thyme, oregano, sumac, and sesame seeds
Za'atar is wild-foraged from Palestinian hillsides — each region's blend is different
Tear pita, scoop labneh with za'atar and olive oil — the combination is ancient
Za'atar + olive oil + bread is the most fundamental Palestinian flavor combination
This breakfast has been eaten in Palestine for thousands of years — unchanged
Palestinian mothers say za'atar makes children smart — it's the first food many learn to love
breakfast.description: Palestine in one bite — thick labneh (strained yoghurt) spread on a plate, pooled with Palestinian olive oil, sprinkled with za'atar (wild-foraged thyme, oregano, sumac, sesame — each region's blend is different). Scooped with pita. This combination has been eaten for thousands of years, unchanged. Palestinian mothers say za'atar makes children smart.

lunch.name: Maqluba (Upside-Down)
instructions: Fry eggplant and cauliflower
Brown meat
Layer in pot: meat, vegetables, rice
Add seasoned water
Cook until done
Flip upside down onto platter
lunch.description: The dramatic flip — rice, meat, and fried vegetables inverted onto a platter.

lunch.name: Maftool (Palestinian Couscous)
instructions: Steam maftool
Cook chicken with chickpeas and spices
Serve maftool topped with chicken and broth
lunch.description: Hand-rolled Palestinian couscous with chicken and chickpeas.

lunch.name: Maqlouba (Upside-Down Rice)
ingredients: Spices: cinnamon, allspice, cardamom, turmeric, cumin
instructions: Maqlouba means 'upside-down' — the pot is flipped onto a serving platter
It's Palestine's celebration rice dish — the dramatic flip is the moment
Layer in a pot: meat first (bottom), then fried vegetables, then seasoned rice
Pour in spiced stock — the rice absorbs the flavor from below
Cook covered until the rice is done — the bottom layer caramelizes slightly
The flip: place a large platter over the pot, invert — the meat is now on top
A successful maqlouba holds its shape — it's a tower of rice with meat on top
The flip is stressful — the family gathers to watch, applauding a clean flip
Garnish with toasted pine nuts and almonds — serve with yoghurt
Maqlouba is Friday lunch food — after mosque, the family gathers
Each cook has their layering preference: eggplant, cauliflower, or both
The spice combination (cinnamon, allspice, cardamom) is distinctly Palestinian
lunch.description: Palestine's dramatic celebration rice — layers of meat, fried eggplant/cauliflower, and spiced rice cooked together, then FLIPPED onto a platter (maqlouba = 'upside-down'). The family gathers to watch the flip — applauding a clean reveal. Garnished with toasted pine nuts, served with yoghurt. Friday lunch after mosque. The spice combination (cinnamon, allspice, cardamom) is distinctly Palestinian.

lunch.name: Musakhan (Sumac Chicken on Taboon Bread)
ingredients: Sumac (ground — the dominant flavor, extremely generous)
Taboon bread (Palestinian flatbread baked on pebbles)
instructions: Musakhan is considered Palestine's national dish — sumac chicken on taboon bread
The sumac is the star — deep purple-red, sour, fruity — used in enormous quantities
Sumac grows wild on Palestinian hillsides — foraging it is a cultural practice
Caramelize a large quantity of onions with sumac and olive oil — they turn deep purple
The onions should be soft, sweet, deeply sumac-stained — this takes time
Roast chicken until golden — then pile the sumac-onion mixture on top
Serve on taboon bread — the flat, pebble-textured bread that bakes in a clay taboon oven
The bread absorbs the olive oil and sumac-onion juices from below
Top with toasted pine nuts — their crunch against the soft onion is the texture
Musakhan is autumn food — the olive oil pressing season coincides with sumac harvest
Eating musakhan is communal — everyone tears bread from the same platter
Musakhan represents the Palestinian olive harvest — the oil is celebrated on the bread
lunch.description: Palestine's national dish — chicken roasted and piled with enormous quantities of caramelized onions stained deep purple with sumac (wild-foraged from Palestinian hillsides), on taboon bread (clay-oven flatbread baked on pebbles) that soaks up the olive oil and sumac juices. Topped with toasted pine nuts. Autumn food: olive pressing season meets sumac harvest. Eaten communally — everyone tears from the same platter.

lunch.name: Freekeh Soup
instructions: Freekeh is roasted young green wheat — a Levantine grain harvested while still green
The wheat is set on fire — the chaff burns away, the moist green kernels survive
This fire-roasting gives freekeh its distinctive smoky, earthy, nutty flavor
Palestinian farmers have been making freekeh for centuries — it's a protected food tradition
Toast the cracked freekeh briefly in oil — it deepens the smoky flavor
Simmer with chicken or lamb, onion, garlic, and warm spices until the grain is tender
The broth becomes earthy and smoky — freekeh releases starch that slightly thickens it
Season with lemon juice — the acid brightens the smoky earthiness
Freekeh is high in fiber and protein — it was the ancient superfood before the term existed
lunch.description: Levantine smoked grain soup — freekeh (young green wheat set on fire — chaff burns, moist kernels survive, gaining a distinctive smoky-nutty flavor) simmered with chicken, cinnamon, and allspice. Palestinian farmers have made freekeh for centuries. High in fiber and protein — the ancient superfood before the term existed. Lemon juice brightens the earthy smokiness.

dinner.name: Makdous (Stuffed Eggplant)
instructions: Boil eggplants briefly
Stuff with walnut-pepper-garlic mixture
Pack in jars, cover with olive oil
Cure 1-2 weeks
dinner.description: Oil-cured stuffed baby eggplants — Palestinian pantry essential.

dinner.name: Mansaf (Lamb in Yogurt)
instructions: Reconstitute jameed into sauce
Simmer lamb in yogurt sauce 90 min
Cook rice
Layer bread, rice, lamb, pour sauce
Top with nuts
dinner.description: Lamb in fermented yogurt sauce over rice.

dinner.name: Mansaf (Lamb in Fermented Yoghurt)
ingredients: Jameed (dried fermented yoghurt — reconstituted into a sauce)
instructions: Mansaf is shared with Jordan — a Bedouin celebration dish eaten across the region
Jameed: fermented dried yoghurt balls — reconstituted in water to make the sauce
The jameed sauce is tangy, salty, complex — it defines the dish
Simmer lamb in the jameed sauce until fall-apart tender
Serve on a large communal platter: flatbread base, rice, lamb, jameed sauce poured over
Topped with toasted nuts — pine nuts and almonds
Mansaf is eaten with the RIGHT HAND — traditionally no utensils
The host serves the guests first — Bedouin hospitality expressed through food
Mansaf appears at weddings, funerals, celebrations — the most important communal meal
In Palestinian Bedouin communities (Negev, Jordan Valley), mansaf is the feast
dinner.description: Bedouin celebration feast — lamb simmered until falling apart in jameed (reconstituted fermented dried yoghurt — tangy, salty, complex), served communally on flatbread with rice and toasted pine nuts. Eaten with the right hand. The host serves guests first — hospitality expressed through food. At weddings, funerals, every important gathering. Shared with Jordan's Bedouin tradition.

dinner.name: Mahashi (Stuffed Vegetables)
ingredients: Zucchini, eggplant, grape leaves, cabbage leaves (for stuffing)
Filling: rice, minced lamb, allspice, cinnamon, salt, pepper
Tomato sauce (or lemon juice for grape leaves)
instructions: Mahashi (stuffed vegetables) is a cornerstone of Palestinian cooking
Hollowing zucchini and eggplant is done with a special coring tool (ma'wara)
The filling: rice and minced lamb seasoned with allspice and cinnamon
Grape leaves (waraq dawali) are stuffed and rolled — a separate art
Cabbage leaves (malfuf) are rolled differently — larger, looser
Pack the stuffed vegetables tightly in a pot — layered
Cover with tomato sauce (or lemon juice for grape leaves) and simmer
The patience required is enormous — hollowing, filling, rolling, packing
Making mahashi is a communal activity — women gather, talk, work together
It represents the agricultural cycle: grape leaves in spring, zucchini in summer
The best mahashi takes all day — the flavors develop in the slow cooking
dinner.description: Palestinian patience embodied — zucchini hollowed with a ma'wara, eggplant cored, grape leaves and cabbage rolled, all stuffed with spiced rice and lamb, packed tight in a pot and simmered in tomato sauce. Making mahashi is communal — women gather, talk, work. Represents the agricultural cycle: grape leaves in spring, zucchini in summer. Takes all day. The flavors reward the patience.

dinner.name: Sayadieh (Fisherman's Rice)
ingredients: White fish (sea bass or grouper — from Gaza's coast)
Onions (caramelized until very dark — the sauce)
Fish stock (from the heads and bones)
instructions: Sayadieh is the fisherman's rice — from Gaza's Mediterranean coast
The dish is defined by the deeply caramelized onion sauce — onions cooked until nearly black
The dark onion purée colors the rice golden-brown and adds intense sweetness
Fish stock from the heads and bones is used to cook the rice — maximum flavor extraction
The fish is fried or poached and placed on top of the rice
Gaza's fishing tradition is ancient — the Mediterranean coast has sustained communities for millennia
Topped with toasted pine nuts and served with lemon wedges
Sayadieh represents Gaza's coastal identity — distinct from the hill-country West Bank cuisine
Each Palestinian region has its culinary identity: coastal Gaza, highland Nablus, Bedouin Negev
dinner.description: Gaza's fisherman's rice — white fish on golden-brown rice colored by deeply caramelized onions (cooked nearly black, then puréed), cooked in fish stock from the heads and bones. Topped with toasted pine nuts, served with lemon. Gaza's ancient Mediterranean fishing tradition. Each Palestinian region has its culinary identity: coastal Gaza, highland Nablus, Bedouin Negev.

snacks.name: Ka'ak al-Quds (Jerusalem Bread)
instructions: Make dough, shape into rings or ovals
Coat with sesame seeds
Bake at 230°C until golden
Fill with za'atar, cheese, or eggs
snacks.description: Sesame-crusted bread rings — Jerusalem street food.

snacks.name: Falafel
ingredients: Dried chickpeas (soaked overnight — NEVER use canned)
Tahini sauce, pickles, tomatoes, pita (for serving)
instructions: Falafel is fundamental to Palestinian street food — eaten daily
The chickpeas must be DRIED, soaked — never canned (canned makes them fall apart)
Process soaked chickpeas with herbs, onion, garlic, spices — a coarse, green-flecked mixture
Shape into balls or patties — the mix should hold together without binders
Deep-fry until dark golden brown — crispy outside, green and fluffy inside
The inside should be VISIBLY GREEN from the herbs — this is the quality mark
Serve in pita with tahini, chopped tomato, cucumber, pickled turnips
Falafel stands are everywhere in Palestinian cities and towns — the everyday lunch
The falafel vendor's technique: shaping and frying with speed and precision
Palestinian falafel is herb-heavy — greener, more fragrant than other regional versions
snacks.description: Palestine's daily street food — dried chickpeas (NEVER canned) ground with parsley, cilantro, dill, and spices, fried dark golden with a visibly GREEN herb-flecked interior. Served in pita with tahini, pickled turnips, and tomato. Palestinian falafel is herb-heavy — greener, more fragrant than other regional versions. The quality mark: a green interior and crispy dark shell.

snacks.name: Ka'ak Al-Quds (Jerusalem Sesame Bread)
ingredients: Bread dough: flour, yeast, water, oil, sugar, mahlab (cherry stone spice)
instructions: Ka'ak al-Quds is Jerusalem's iconic sesame bread — sold by vendors at Damascus Gate
The oblong bread ring is covered in sesame seeds — the aroma of toasting sesame is the signal
The dough contains mahlab (ground cherry pit kernel) — a distinctive Middle Eastern spice
Mahlab gives a subtle bitter-almond, cherry-like flavor — unique to this bread
The ka'ak vendors at Damascus Gate (Bab al-Amud) are a Jerusalem institution
The bread is eaten plain or filled: za'atar, cheese, boiled egg, or falafel stuffed inside
Morning commuters grab ka'ak — the grab-and-go breakfast of Jerusalem
The circular shape and sesame coating are unmistakable — recognizable across the region
Ka'ak al-Quds is a symbol of Palestinian Jerusalem — cultural identity in bread form
snacks.description: Jerusalem's sesame bread icon — oblong bread rings coated in sesame seeds, made with mahlab (cherry stone spice giving a subtle cherry-almond flavor), sold by vendors at Damascus Gate (Bab al-Amud). The grab-and-go breakfast of Jerusalem. Filled with za'atar, cheese, or egg. Cultural identity in bread form — a symbol of Palestinian Jerusalem.

snacks.name: Fatayer (Spinach Pies)
ingredients: Dough: flour, yeast, olive oil, water
Filling: spinach (chopped), onion, lemon juice, sumac, pine nuts
instructions: Fatayer are triangular spinach pies — baked, golden, filled with lemony spinach
The spinach is mixed with onion, lemon juice, and sumac — the filling is tart and green
Pine nuts add crunch and richness inside the spinach filling
The dough is olive oil enriched — soft, slightly chewy, golden when baked
Shaped into triangles: three corners pinched together, leaving the top slightly open
Baked until golden — the spinach filling peeks through the top
Fatayer are made in large batches — dozens at a time, eaten over several days
The lemon-sumac tang of the spinach against the soft bread is the pleasure
Palestinian women make fatayer communally — a social baking event
Fatayer freeze well — practical for feeding large families
snacks.description: Palestinian triangular spinach pies — soft olive-oil dough pinched into three-cornered shapes around a filling of spinach, onion, lemon juice, sumac, and pine nuts. Baked golden with the filling peeking through the top. Made communally in large batches — a social baking event. The lemon-sumac tang against soft bread. Freeze well for feeding large families.

desserts.name: Knafeh Nabulsi
instructions: Butter knafeh dough
Press half in pan, add cheese, top with rest
Bake until golden and crispy
Flip, drizzle with syrup
Top with crushed pistachios
desserts.description: Nablus's famous crispy cheese pastry in sweet syrup.

desserts.name: Knafeh Nabulsieh (Nablus Cheese Pastry)
ingredients: Nabulsi cheese (desalted — sweet, stretchy white cheese from Nablus)
Sugar syrup (atar — sugar, water, rose water, lemon juice)
Orange food coloring (traditional — the signature color)
instructions: Knafeh nabulsieh is Palestine's most celebrated dessert — from Nablus
Nablus has been making knafeh for centuries — the city owns this dessert
The Nabulsi cheese is the key — a white brine cheese (desalted for knafeh) that melts and stretches
The cheese pulls in long strings when the knafeh is cut — the cheese pull IS the show
The kadaif (shredded pastry) is mixed with ghee and pressed into the pan — bottom layer
Nabulsi cheese is placed on top — then baked until the bottom is crispy and the cheese melts
Flipped onto a platter — the crispy golden layer is now on top
Soaked in sugar syrup (atar) scented with rose water — sweet, fragrant, dripping
The orange-red color of the pastry is traditional — food coloring is the norm
Topped with crushed pistachios — green against orange
Knafeh is eaten warm — the cheese must be stretchy, the pastry crispy
Nablus knafeh vendors serve it for breakfast — yes, cheese pastry soaked in syrup for breakfast
The Nablus knafeh shops are destinations — people drive hours for the best
desserts.description: Nablus' crown jewel — shredded kadaif pastry crisped in ghee, layered over stretchy Nabulsi cheese (a white brine cheese unique to Nablus), baked until the cheese melts and pulls in strings, flipped, and soaked in rose water syrup. The cheese pull when cut IS the show. Orange-tinted (traditional), topped with pistachios. Nablus has made knafeh for centuries — the city owns this dessert. People drive hours for the best shops.

desserts.name: Qatayef (Ramadan Pancakes)
ingredients: Batter: flour, yeast, sugar, water, baking powder
Filling: sweet cheese (akkawi — desalted) or walnuts with cinnamon and sugar
instructions: Qatayef are Ramadan's dessert — stuffed pancakes that appear ONLY during Ramadan
The batter is poured on a griddle — cooked on ONE SIDE ONLY (the bubbles side stays raw)
The raw side is sticky — it's used to seal the pancake around the filling
Fill with sweet cheese or walnut-cinnamon-sugar mixture
Pinch the edges shut — the pancake becomes a half-moon
Deep-fry until golden, then soak in rose water sugar syrup
Qatayef are eaten after iftar (the breaking of the fast) — sweet energy after a day of fasting
During Ramadan, qatayef vendors appear on every street — the seasonal market
The sound of frying qatayef and the smell of rose water syrup IS Ramadan evenings
Making qatayef at home is a family activity — everyone fills and pinches
desserts.description: Ramadan's exclusive dessert — pancakes cooked on one side only (the raw side seals), stuffed with sweet cheese or walnut-cinnamon, fried golden, and soaked in rose water syrup. Qatayef appear ONLY during Ramadan — vendors set up on every street for the season. Eaten after iftar (breaking the fast). The sound of frying and the scent of rose water syrup IS Ramadan evening.

drinks.name: Arabic Coffee
instructions: Boil in dallah with cardamom
Serve in small finjan cups

drinks.name: Qamar al-Din (Apricot Drink)
instructions: Soak apricot leather overnight
Blend until smooth
Add sugar and rose water
Serve cold
drinks.description: Apricot nectar drink — a Ramadan tradition.

drinks.name: Sahlab (Orchid Root Hot Milk)
ingredients: Sahlab powder (from orchid root tubers — the thickener)
instructions: Sahlab is the winter hot drink — thick, creamy, floral, warming
Made from the ground tubers of an orchid species — sahlab powder thickens milk
Heat milk, stir in sahlab powder and sugar — it thickens to a pudding-like consistency
Add rose water — the floral aroma rises from the hot cup
Top with cinnamon, crushed pistachios, and shredded coconut
Sahlab vendors appear in winter — especially in Jerusalem's Old City
The drink is thick enough to eat with a spoon — halfway between drink and dessert
Sahlab is shared across the Levant and Turkey — called salep in Turkish
In Palestine, sahlab warms cold winter nights — the comfort drink of December and January
drinks.description: Palestine's winter warmer — milk thickened with sahlab (ground orchid root tubers) into a pudding-like consistency, scented with rose water, topped with cinnamon, pistachios, and coconut. Thick enough to eat with a spoon. Sahlab vendors appear in Jerusalem's Old City in winter. Shared across the Levant and Turkey. The comfort drink of December and January.
